title: What Takes 20 Years to Build Takes 5 Minutes to Destroy
summary: I think we’ve all heard many variations of the adage, “It takes 20 years to build a reputation, but only five minutes to destroy it.” A good name that has been established through many years of honor, success, or skilled leadership can be ruined in a moment when an act of immorality comes to light. See Also A La Carte (2/13) The Sinner’s Opinion of Himself The True Character of Unbelief
content: I think we’ve all heard many variations of the adage, “It takes 20 years to build a reputation, but only five minutes to destroy it.” A good name that has been established through many years of honor, success, or skilled leadership can be ruined in a moment when an act of immorality comes to light. Until a couple of weeks ago, Jensen Huang seemed to be on top of the world. While Nvidia, the company he co-founded, had long been a Silicon Valley success story, the rise of AI had driven it to new heights of success and its CEO to new heights of prosperity. Nvidia became the most valuable company in the world, its market capitalization of nearly $6 trillion surpassing even Apple’s. Huang’s net worth soared to over $200 billion, making him one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the richest men in history. His two children have advanced positions within the company and his wife of more than 40 years distributes vast sums of money through their charitable foundation. Huang carefully curated his reputation and, as is so often the case in Silicon Valley, his image, with his slick black leather jackets becoming his trademark. Today, of course, Huang is no longer CEO of Nvidia or anything else. He was forced to resign after it came to light that he had engaged in extramarital affairs with multiple women, one of whom is allegedly a Chinese spy and another of whom is reportedly a subordinate within Nvidia. His image was shattered in a moment, and his reputation is now in tatters. The company lost over half a trillion dollars of value in the aftermath—value that was subtracted from Huang’s wealth, of course, but also from that of everyday investors whose wealth is far more modest. Pictures of his wife and children were splashed all over the news, and stories about his exploits were printed in every major media outlet in the world. The harm to his reputation is beyond repair, yet must pale in comparison to the harm and shame he has brought to his family. I hope that as Huang ponders what has become of his life, he has the wisdom to ask this: was it worth it? I hope each one of us asks the same, for Huang is not the first person to be tempted to grave sin , nor the first to succumb to temptation. In different ways and to different degrees, that is a battle we all fight every day. I have no experience of committing adultery, but I understand that it is exhilarating, and that doing what is forbidden delivers a great rush. And I suppose it must be exhilarating, for why else would a person risk so much to pursue it? Why else would a person do something that so defies common sense? Why else would a person gamble everything for the sake of illicit, fleeting pleasures? News reports describe him, in his final days at the company, calling himself “a piece of [expletive].” And while I wouldn’t phrase it that way, he’s not wrong that this situation has exposed him as what he truly is, and it’s actually far worse than the way he describes it. I might choose the word “wretch” to describe him, and not just him, but all of us. We are all wretches, for we are all wretched, people who trade short-term pleasure for long-term pain and fleeting joys for enduring sorrows. Sin makes us act like madmen, for sin is madness. And it leaves us wretched—desperately unhappy and in the sorriest of states. There has never been a sin that was more wise than foolish. There has never been a sin that delivered more gratification than the satisfaction of obedience. There has never been a sin that was worth more than the honor of a good name and an upstanding reputation. Thankfully, there has never been a sin that is beyond Jesus’s capacity to forgive. Though time and again we, like Huang, succumb to temptation, time and again Jesus forgives those who humble themselves before him to confess their sin and ask his forgiveness. May we all have the wisdom to see ourselves in Huang and to see in him a vivid example of the reality that sin promises joy while delivering sorr

Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a couple of daily Advent devotionals, Greg Koukl’s Street Smarts , David Gibson’s Living Life Backward , Dane Ortlund’s Deeper , and more. Swain remembers and honors John Allen Chau. “There has been plenty of discussion around John’s level of wisdom and preparedness. Many feel these were lacking. I will admit that landing on an island whose inhabitants are known to be violent toward outsiders is unwise. The wiser thing would’ve been for him to invest his savings in a mutual fund for forty years. How short-sighted of him. In the words of one of the five in Ecuador who preceded him in martyrdom, ‘He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.’ John was no fool.” How to Experience Gospel Transformation. Take 5-10 minutes each night, and try to choose one thing (not a million things) that needs repentance from your day. It’s very important that you go beyond just naming your sin to God, here. It’s important to name your sin (even out loud!), but that’s not going to transform you. What will transform you is learning to practice reconciliation with God, through the gospel.” The Quiet Voice. Catherine Mackenzie was one of those people who enjoyed the quiet that came to her life when Outlook crashed. “Although almost everything I had planned that day depended on email, and almost none of it got done, I actually talked to my colleagues. We caught up properly, in a way our inboxes don’t usually leave room for. I sat beside the designer instead of messaging her on Teams, and we all shared jokes and discussed our favourite period dramas.” She goes on to draw some observations from the marriage of John and Polly Newton. What We Get Wrong About the Tears of Jesus. John Piper addresses (and corrects, I suppose) a misplaced emphasis when it comes to a famous story from the life of Jesus—weeping outside the tomb of his friend Lazarus. I Thought Adultery Had Been Approved. I thought adultery had become widely acceptable. How can a company part with such a genius merely because of consensual sex out of marriage? Supposedly, this was a victimless crime that should not inhibit the rise of super duper intelligence, especially earning trillions.” The Singularity Will Never Happen. Some people are concerned that with the rise of AI we are heading to the point of singularity, but Justin Poythress explains why that will never happen. “We know the future will look dramatically different, but we’re only beginning to conceive the ways in which AI will reshape it. content: Tuesday is the day most publishers release their new books, so each week I let you know what has just come our way from the publishers I follow most closely. This is a big week, thanks largely to Christian Focus, which releases its whole November list in one go. It also brings a new edition of J. I. Packer’s Truth and Power , Matthew Westerholm’s Biblical Worship , Randy Alcorn’s major book on what the Bible says about animals, and the newest volume in the Reformed Expository Commentary. There are also several new academic works and a number of books for children. In each case, I’ve included the publisher’s description. Books for Everyone Crossway Biblical Worship A Christ-Centered Practical Theology Matthew Westerholm Endorsed by: Thomas R. Schreiner, Ryanne J. Molinari, Joseph R. Crider, Brian J. Tabb, and Zac Hicks Publisher’s description Humans are made to worship, but as sinners, the most we can offer God is imperfect praise. In the Old Testament, people used various symbols and rituals to show devotion, but these flawed offerings would find their ultimate fulfillment in Jesus, the perfect worshiper. So, what should biblical worship look like for redeemed people today? Matthew Westerholm gives churches a unified vision for worship by studying its different expressions throughout salvation history. First, he presents a biblical theology of worship from Genesis to Christ. Next, Westerholm defines proper worship as acknowledging God’s creating power, generous faithfulness, and purposeful commission. Finally, he offers readers practical guidance about where, when, and how to worship today. Written to encourage the entire congregation, this book celebrates how Christ’s atoning work transforms worship from ritualistic obligation to joyful expression. Buy it at Amazon or Westminster Books . Christian Focus Shattered Dreams and God’s Plan The Joseph Narrative in Genesis 37–50 Dale Ralph Davis Endorsed by: Sam Emadi and Harrison Perkins Publisher’s description Dale Ralph Davis gives us a rich, pastoral exploration of Joseph’s story—where shattered dreams, hidden providence, and unshakable grace collide. With clarity, wit, and deep theological insight, Davis brings Genesis 37–50 to life, showing how God works through chaos, silence, and suffering to accomplish his purposes. Perfect for personal study, preaching, or group discussion, this book invites readers to see their own struggles through the lens of God’s faithful plan. Whether you’re navigating your own “Genesis 37” season or seeking a deeper understanding of Scripture, Shattered Dreams and God’s Plan will strengthen your faith and renew your confidence in the God who never abandons His plans—or His people. Buy it at Amazon . IVP Truth and Power The Place of Scripture in the Christian Life J. I. Packer Endorsed by: Kevin J. content: I was glad to return home safely after an extremely enjoyable weekend in San Diego with the men of Compass Bible Church. It was a fitting end to my speaking engagements for the year. I’m now settled back into my home office to get cracking on some major book projects. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a variety of books, and among them you’ll find a couple of relatively new titles from P&R: Pray with Your Eyes Open and You Are Not Alone . You’ll also find Mark Vroegop’s ultra-popular Dark Clouds, Deep Mercy and several other options. Recommended Reading Classroom Apologetics. I think you’ll be encouraged to read of Joshua Budimlic’s extraordinary experience in a Canadian public school classroom. “In the Lord’s timing, the morning of September 11th, 2025, was the day I taught my first lesson to a class of Grade 11 Law students—Charlie Kirk had been murdered the day before. As you can imagine, Charlie’s death overshadowed any plans I’d previously made to open my lecture with a discussion of 9/11 and its lasting implications, or the then-recent murder of Iryna Zarutska on a North Carolina light-rail train just a few weeks prior. It was only the second week of the new school year, and already the darkness was beginning to gather.” Can We Legitimately Judge a Person’s Faith? Stephen Kneale answers an important question: Can we legitimately judge another person’s faith? He explains why this is not merely legitimate, but necessary. “We all know liars exists, wolves do run around and many, though no doubt sincere, can be self-deceived. Some Christians can be quick to take every word at face value and easily fooled whilst others, albeit often out of sincere motive, lead people to believe in unbiblical theology and gospels full of half-truths that can leave genuine people further away from Jesus than they realise.” Lord, Why Am I Still Here? Peter Witkowski: “Few questions can appear as esoteric and yet prove as profoundly practical as the question: ‘Lord, Why am I still here?’ It is a question that seminary students with little life experience can talk over into the early hours of the morning as they sip energy drinks. It is a question that the newly minted widower feels throughout the recesses of his soul as he selects a coffin for his beloved bride. And it is a question that Jesus answers…” The World Is Always Burning. Andrea Sanborn is correct: it does feel like the world is burning right now. Yet in some ways, it is always true that the world is burning. “Does it seem like the world is burning to you? From droughts to floods, wars and riots…sometimes it feels like we are falling apart. Like we are falling apart from each other. From common sense or sanity, even. From God. It’s disconcerting, certainly. Flat-out frightening at times. At best, we live with a low-level anxiety humming in our spirits, wondering how close the flames will creep to our homes. The truth is, the world has always been burning. Burning up. Burning down. Only now, technology allows us to witness the flames in every corner.” Frank Peretti, the 40th Anniversary of This Present Darkness, and Memories From Years of Friendship. I perhaps don’t feel quite as positive about This Present Darkness as Randy Alcorn does, but I still enjoyed reading about his friendship with Frank Peretti. It’s hard to believe that the book is 40 years old! The Best Way to Serve Your Local Church. “‘I really want to find a way to plug in and serve the church.’ I overheard this comment about a decade ago as a church member spoke to one of our pastors. I loved the sincerity and desire of this brother, but I wondered what our pastor was going to say. I leaned in and listened extra close because I was genuinely curious.” The answer was a good one. title: Carta Pastoral de los Obispos de México con motivo del centenario del inicio de la resistencia cristera – Infovaticana Blogs
summary: A cien años del inicio de la resistencia cristera, los obispos mexicanos proponen leer aquel doloroso episodio histórico desde la verdad, la libertad de conciencia, la reconciliación y el compromiso d
content: A cien años del inicio de la resistencia cristera, los obispos mexicanos proponen leer aquel doloroso episodio histórico desde la verdad, la libertad de conciencia, la reconciliación y el compromiso de una fe dispuesta a hacerse servicio A cien años del inicio de la resistencia cristera, los obispos de México han dirigido al país una carta pastoral que busca recuperar uno de los episodios más dolorosos, complejos y controvertidos de la historia nacional sin convertirlo en instrumento de revancha, polarización o legitimación de la violencia. Bajo el título ¡Viva Cristo Rey! Su fe, nuestra memoria; su testimonio, nuestra misión, el documento propone una lectura histórica, teológica, espiritual, jurídica y pastoral de aquellos acontecimientos, pero, sobre todo, formula una pregunta dirigida a los creyentes de nuestro tiempo: ¿Qué significa hoy mantener viva una fe por la que otros estuvieron dispuestos a entregar la existencia? La carta no celebra la guerra ni presenta la resistencia armada como modelo de acción cristiana para el presente. Su punto de partida es otro, recordar la fidelidad de un pueblo que, en medio de la persecución, continuó rezando en sus hogares, bautizando a sus hijos, protegiendo a sus sacerdotes, celebrando clandestinamente los sacramentos y defendiendo la libertad de conciencia frente a un Estado que pretendió administrar las convicciones religiosas como si fueran una concesión del poder. Los obispos establecen desde el comienzo una diferencia indispensable entre el conflicto bélico, con sus errores, excesos, responsabilidades y heridas, y el testimonio de quienes murieron sin renunciar a su fe. Los mártires, subraya el documento, no son recordados porque hubieran matado por Cristo, sino porque murieron por Él y, en numerosos casos, perdonaron a sus verdugos. No se trata de recuperar un grito de guerra, sino la fuerza espiritual de una conciencia que se negó a ser sometida. El episcopado propone un triple ejercicio de memoria histórica, valoración del martirio y compromiso cristiano con la vida, la dignidad humana y la paz. Al recorrer la carta aparece una convicción transversal, la memoria solo es auténticamente cristiana cuando conduce a la conversión, ayuda a sanar las heridas, impide la repetición de las injusticias y se transforma en misión. Ese propósito exige comenzar por “un breve recuento del conflicto religioso”, título del primer capítulo y punto de entrada para entender que la confrontación no surgió repentinamente en 1926. Sus antecedentes se remontan a la formación del Estado mexicano después de la Independencia, cuando comenzaron a enfrentarse dos proyectos de nación. Uno reconocía al catolicismo como fundamento del orden social; el otro pretendía limitar la influencia institucional de la Iglesia para consolidar un Estado liberal, soberano y progresivamente secular. La Constitución de 1857 y las Leyes de Reforma representaron un momento decisivo en ese proceso. Establecieron la separación entre la Iglesia y el Estado, limitaron la propiedad eclesiástica y modificaron la presencia de la institución religiosa en la educación y la vida civil. Para sus promotores fueron disposiciones indispensables para modernizar al país; para la Iglesia y numerosos católicos significaron una intervención hostil sobre espacios que consideraban esenciales para su identidad y misión. La carta reconoce, sin embargo, que la secularización no ocurrió de manera inmediata ni eliminó el profundo arraigo del catolicismo en la vida nacional. La fe continuó presente en las costumbres, las familias, la educación, las fiestas y las formas comunitarias de organización. En ese contexto cobró fuerza el catolicismo social, inspirado en buena medida por la encíclica Rerum novarum de 1891. Surgieron organizaciones obreras, asociaciones juveniles y femeninas, cajas de ahorro para campesinos, escuelas nocturnas, centros de ayuda mutua, medios de comunicación y proyectos de participación política. title: RED WEEK PER RICORDARE I CRISTIANI PERSEGUITATI
summary: Anche quest’anno, nonostante il disinteresse dei media, dal 15 al 22 novembre la Fondazione Pontificia Aiuto alla Chiesa che Soffre ha dato vita al Red Week per ricordare che in tutto il mondo milioni
content: Anche quest’anno, nonostante il disinteresse dei media, dal 15 al 22 novembre la Fondazione Pontificia Aiuto alla Chiesa che Soffre ha dato vita al Red Week per ricordare che in tutto il mondo milioni di persone sono discriminate o perseguitate per la loro fede, in particolare le tante comunità cristiane che vivono in contesti dove la loro libertà religiosa subisce gravi violazioni. Per farlo, luoghi di culto, monumenti ed edifici pubblici in questa settimana si sono illuminate di rosso in tante nazioni contemporaneamente in occasione della Red Week, Dal 2015, sono stati illuminati luoghi di culto e monumenti fra i più iconici del mondo: dalla Fontana di Trevi a Roma al monumento del Cristo Redentore di Rio de Janeiro, dalla Basilica della Sagrada Familia di Barcellona a quella del Sacro Cuore di Parigi. La libertà religiosa in pericolo. Il Rapporto sulla libertà religiosa nel mondo 2025 di Aiuto alla Chiesa che Soffre evidenzia come in 62 Paesi si siano verificate violazioni sistematiche della libertà religiosa: 24 Paesi rientrano nella categoria più grave, ovvero quella di “persecuzione”, e 38 in quella di “discriminazione”. Complessivamente, oltre 5,4 miliardi di persone vivono in contesti in cui la libertà di religione è seriamente compromessa. 413 milioni di cristiani vivono in Paesi in cui la libertà religiosa è gravemente violata; di questi, circa 220 milioni risiedono in nazioni in cui sono direttamente esposti a persecuzioni. Regimi autoritari, violenza jihadista, nazionalismi religiosi e criminalità organizzata rappresentano oggi le principali minacce. Voci dimenticate: due serate tra musica e testimonianza a Milano e Roma Tra gli appuntamenti centrali della Red Week 2026 si sono svolte due serate di Voci dimenticate, il 16 novembre a Milano nella Basilica di Santa Maria delle Grazie, e il 21 novembre a Roma nella Basilica di San Saba. Chi lo desidera potrà contribuire, con una donazione libera, ai progetti di Aiuto alla Chiesa che Soffre a beneficio dei cristiani perseguitati. A Milano il pubblico ha assistito al concerto del Coro Filarmonico G.B. Pergolesi e dell’Orchestra Filarmonica Amadeus, diretti dal Maestro Gianmario Cavallaro; in programma brani del repertorio barocco, con musiche di Vivaldi, Torelli e Händel. Nella capitale il Coro Città di Roma, diretto dal Maestro Mauro Marchetti, ha proposto invece un percorso musicale con musiche di Mozart, Bach e Pergolesi. Ospite di entrambi gli appuntamenti è stata una donna che ha vissuto personalmente il dramma della persecuzione. La giovane sarà accompagnata da Don Joseph Fidelis Bature, sacerdote della diocesi nigeriana di Maiduguri e direttore del Trauma Center. La struttura, sostenuta dai benefattori di ACS, offre assistenza psicologica, spirituale e sociale alle vittime del gruppo terroristico islamista Boko Haram, accompagnandole in un percorso di guarigione e reinserimento nella comunità. Le loro toccanti testimonianze hanno raccontato la violenza che continua a colpire migliaia di persone e le occasioni di rinascita rese possibili dalla solidarietà di numerosi benefattori, italiani e internazionali. Le donazioni raccolte durante i due eventi di Milano e Roma sosterranno in particolare un progetto finanziato da ACS nella diocesi nigeriana di Minna, nel cui territorio le comunità cristiane vivono sotto la minaccia di attacchi armati, sequestri e violenze. L’iniziativa aiuterà 200 donne, uomini e bambini sopravvissuti alla violenza a ricostruire la propria vita attraverso il sostegno psicologico, il rafforzamento dei legami con la comunità e, per gli adulti, il recupero dell’autonomia economica. Il progetto prevede inoltre la formazione di circa 60 figure di riferimento delle comunità locali, tra cui sacerdoti e autorità, affinché sappiano riconoscere i bisogni delle persone più vulnerabili e offrire loro un sostegno adeguato. title: Cristiani perseguitati : Acs , a Bologna la Basilica di San Petronio illuminata di rosso per non dimenticare
summary: In occasione della “Red Week 2026. Non dimentichiamo i cristiani perseguitati”, la Basilica di San Petronio a Bologna sarà illuminata di rosso dalla Fondazione “Aiuto alla Chiesa che soffre” (Acs) per
content: In occasione della “Red Week 2026. Non dimentichiamo i cristiani perseguitati”, la Basilica di San Petronio a Bologna sarà illuminata di rosso dalla Fondazione “Aiuto alla Chiesa che soffre” (Acs) per ricordare i cristiani perseguitati. Alle 18 di domenica 22 novembre, nel Santuario di Santa Maria della Vita, saranno proposte le testimonianze di don Joseph Fidelis, Direttore del “Trauma Center” di Maiduguri (Nigeria) e di Justina, vittima delle violenze di Boko Haram. Seguirà la celebrazione della Messa e, al termine, si raggiungerà il sagrato della Basilica di San Petronio. “La luce rossa è un simbolo forte – sottolinea Massimo Pinardi, Direttore dell’Ufficio diocesano Amministrativo e Beni Culturali – perché ci ricorda il sangue dei martiri. Questa iniziativa ci aiuterà a fare memoria, ma anche a dimostrare solidarietà e vicinanza alle popolazioni che tengono viva la fiammella della fede in Gesù Cristo nel mondo. Quello del martirio è, infatti, un concetto che ci sembra lontano, eppure sono tanti i luoghi nel mondo dove le persone vengono discriminate, emarginate o addirittura uccise per il solo fatto di essere cristiane”.
author: agensir.it

title: Bolivia . Los obispos rechazan el proyecto de ley de eutanasia : Una sociedad se mide por cómo trata a sus miembros más débiles , no por cómo se deshace de ellos
summary: En esta crónica semanal sobre Hispanoamérica recogemos noticias destacadas ocurridas en la región compuesta por países hermanados en la Hispanidad (que tienen en común su fe cristiana, su cultura y su
content: En esta crónica semanal sobre Hispanoamérica recogemos noticias destacadas ocurridas en la región compuesta por países hermanados en la Hispanidad (que tienen en común su fe cristiana, su cultura y su lengua y cuya patrona es la Virgen del Pilar) y tratando de defender los principios no negociables -vida, familia, libertad de enseñanza, bien común y libertad religiosa- establecidos por el Papa Benedicto XVI para una acción política basada en el humanismo cristiano. Esta semana empezamos en Bolivia para defender el derecho a la vida frente a la eutanasia. En ese país, el diputado Diego Brañez, de la formación APB Súmate (centroderecha) presentó el pasado el 11 de agosto ante la Cámara de Diputados el proyecto de Ley de Cuidados Paliativos, Muerte Digna y Eutanasia, que pretende permitir la eutanasia bajo determinadas condiciones a personas con enfermedades irreversibles. Recordemos que Bolivia está gobernada por el presidente Rodrigo Paz Pereira, del Partido Demócrata Cristiano (PDC). Asumió la Presidencia el 8 de noviembre de 2025. Los obispos bolivianos rechazaron este proyecto mediante un comunicado titulado ‘El valor sagrado de la vida y el rechazo a la eutanasia’, en el que recordaron “la profunda trascendencia humana y espiritual de la dignidad del ser humano y el valor de la vida, rechazando la eutanasia y reafirmando su compromiso de servicio y acompañamiento a través de un trato digno y fraterno a todo enfermo”. En ese sentido, los obispos subrayaron que “la vida es un don sagrado de Dios, no es una propiedad de la que podamos disponer nosotros”, por lo que “nadie tiene el derecho de poner fin de manera deliberada a su propia existencia o a la de un hermano frágil”. Ante los argumentos legislativos que proponen la eutanasia como alivio del sufrimiento, los prelados sostienen que la verdadera compasión “no consiste en provocar la muerte” para evitar el sufrimiento, sino en “sentir con el otro” mediante el amor, el acompañamiento y el cuidado, y nunca el descarte. “Aunque la curación médica no siempre sea posible, el cuidado y el acompañamiento humano, espiritual y sanitario lo son hasta el último suspiro”, destacan, abogando “firmemente por la promoción y el acceso a los cuidados paliativos, que alivian eficazmente el dolor físico, respetan el proceso natural de la muerte y cubren las necesidades emocionales y espirituales del enfermo y de su familia”. En ese contexto, llaman a las autoridades a “que los cuidados paliativos sean accesibles a los que más lo necesitan”, alertando que “legalizar o normalizar la eutanasia debilita el tejido social y presiona, de forma directa o indirecta, a los más enfermos, ancianos y vulnerables, haciéndoles sentir que su vida ha perdido valor”. “Una sociedad se mide por cómo trata a sus miembros más débiles, no por cómo se deshace de ellos”, enfatizan, exhortando a toda la sociedad a ser “artesanos de la vida y de la esperanza” y a dar testimonio del inmenso valor de la vida. Nos vamos a México, donde la Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación (SCJN) ha avalado la instalación de un nacimiento de Jesucristo en un edificio público del municipio de Mocochá, en Yucatán, tras decidir por ocho votos frente a uno el sobreseimiento del recurso, informa Ewtnnews. La demanda, presentada por un ciudadano que consideraba que la representación vulneraba el principio de Estado laico y derechos como la libertad religiosa y la no discriminación, se refería a un nacimiento colocado en diciembre de 2020 y difundido en redes sociales por el Ayuntamiento. La decisión, adoptada el 19 de octubre, se fundamentó en que el demandante había desistido del recurso. Con ello, quedan descartados los tres procesos judiciales contra nacimientos instalados en espacios públicos de distintos municipios de Yucatán. Luis Barrera, gerente de Campañas en la plataforma Actívate, consideró la decisión de la SCJN como “una muy buena noticia”. title_zh: 良十四世提醒我们，基督的王权是和平的王权。

title: From Post-Punk to German Techno—A Musical Journey
summary: By Mark Ellis — Known for his scholarship, journalism, and voice, Brian C. Nixon has another creative life—one that spans more than three decades of songwriting, recording, and musical exploration. Nixon is perhaps best known for his academic work at Veritas International University, his books, and his journalism for God Reports, ASSIST News Service, and other media […]  The post  From Post-Punk to German Techno—A Musical Journey  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Mark Ellis — Known for his scholarship, journalism, and voice, Brian C. Nixon has another creative life—one that spans more than three decades of songwriting, recording, and musical exploration. Brian Nixon Nixon is perhaps best known for his academic work at Veritas International University , his books, and his journalism for God Reports , ASSIST News Service , and other media outlets. His voice has also reached listeners across the country through his former involvement with the radio program To Every Man an Answer (later known as Pastors’ Perspective ) and, more recently, Paratus , a program devoted to developing a biblical worldview. What may surprise those familiar with Nixon’s academic and journalistic work is that he is also an accomplished musician and songwriter whose musical journey spans more than 30 years. In his forthcoming book, A Beautiful Defense: How Aesthetics Points to God , co-written with Dr. Patrick Zukeran and scheduled for release in 2027 , Nixon explores the relationship between beauty, faith, and the creative process. In anticipation of the book’s release, I spoke with Nixon about his musical beginnings, his creative influences, and his unexpected venture into German electronic music. Tell me about your early musical journey. I grew up in a musical family. Music was part of my everyday life. During high school, I formed a band with some friends that eventually signed with an independent record label in the San Francisco Bay Area. We released only one record, but several of the other members went on to successful careers in the music industry. One became involved in founding Stones Throw Records, an influential independent label known for its underground hip-hop and experimental music. It was an exciting time. We were young, creative, and discovering what music could be. What did you do after the band broke up? I continued my college education, eventually transferring to California State University, Stanislaus. There, I met another group of musicians, and we formed a band called Canterbury. We ended up winning a Bay Area battle-of-the-bands competition, which was exciting. But rather than continuing in that direction, we decided to pursue something with a more intentional ministry focus. That led to the formation of Widow’s Mite . Widow’s Mite eventually signed with Rick Wakeman, the legendary keyboardist of Yes. Interestingly, that connection also introduced me to journalist Dan Wooding, who wrote Wakeman’s first biography. That relationship eventually opened the door for me to write for ASSIST News Service . So, in a rather unexpected way, my musical career helped launch my journalism career. Widow’s Mite After college, did you continue writing music? Absolutely. I still write music today. My compositions range from jazz and pop to what I call tone poems —short instrumental works that emphasize mood, atmosphere, and musical expression. Some are experimental, while others are much more accessible. I’ve always enjoyed exploring different musical forms rather than staying within a single genre. Interestingly, some of my recent compositions have been selected for rotation by a German online radio station. And here’s the surprising part: they’re German electronic and techno-influenced songs. I’ve been experimenting with AI-assisted production, including using a synthesized female vocalist to interpret my compositions. Did you say German techno? (Laughs.) I know. It sounds funny, doesn’t it? But there’s a story behind it. Recently, I took a deep dive into the music of Kraftwerk, the pioneering German electronic band. I was familiar with their work during high school in the early 1980s because they had influenced so many of the post-punk bands I was listening to at the time. I decided to revisit their entire catalog, and I was blown away all over again. They were years ahead of their time. Their approach to rhythm, synthesizers, repetition, and technology helped shape entire genres of contemporary music.

content: By Charles Gardner — Charles and Linda on their wedding day My wife Linda had no idea of the Jewish background of her employers during the 1970s and 80s. She just knew that she loved working for them and only left to follow God’s call to work with children. So we travelled down to London for an exhibition of the Salmon and Gluckstein dynasty, and the story of how these resilient Jewish families fled violent persecution in Eastern Europe to build what became the largest catering company in the world known as J Lyons & Co. Linda worked there as a home economist from 1977-1984 but it was only much later that she learnt of the Jewish nature of the firm that once literally fed Britain with its teashops and corner houses on every high street, and its products in every home, Linda playing her part through her cooking and marketing skills. A few years later, after graduating from Bible College in Bournemouth, she worked at a prayer and reconciliation centre in Northern Ireland where she was introduced to the importance of the Christian faith’s Jewish roots, as a result of which she took a study tour of Israel to learn more. And on a second trip to the Holy Land ten years later, she got more than she bargained for. At Cana in Galilee, where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding, Linda was given a vision of her own wedding. And we met on a blind date six months later! Though having Jewish ancestry myself, I grew up knowing nothing about it. But I learnt more later, especially after becoming a Christian in my early twenties, as Linda had done. It helped that I had a Jewish believer as my early mentor, and I became increasingly aware of the significance of our Jewish heritage, about which I now write prolifically. Meanwhile Linda, who has been teaching Christianity in Doncaster area schools for over 30 years, also now teaches about Judaism as it forms the context into which Christ came to us, fulfilling all the laws and promises of the Old Testament. So in both our cases, we were kept in the dark about very important aspects of our lives – until the Lord shone his light on the truth. Which brings me to the Christian Church as a whole, especially in the UK. We have known very little, if anything, of our faith’s Jewish roots or of God’s ongoing purposes for Israel. This needs to change – and fast! For we are surely hurtling towards the Messiah’s Second Coming like a high-speed train, in danger of coming off the rails with the rest of humanity if we fail to get to grips with how we Christians fit into the unfolding picture of global opposition to tiny Israel. What is our role as we watch antisemitism spread across the globe like wildfire? Do we just sit and watch, or write it off as having nothing to do with us, and remain silent? Or do we stand up to be counted as those who refuse to salute the new Nazism that portrays itself as anti-Zionism – a Confessing Church walking the way of the cross for God’s chosen people? My questions come as renewed calls are made for an independent inquiry into antisemitism at the BBC following news that Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon has won £400,000 in compensation from the broadcaster. Lucie’s career is said to have unravelled after she raised concerns about antisemitism within the BBC, though the latter have not admitted to any fault. This is highly significant as millions of UK Christians are (where Israel is concerned) probably more influenced by what they hear from our national broadcaster than what they read in the Bible. title: New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran
summary: By Howard Cooper — Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, says he plans to take his oath of office on a Quran when the new Congress convenes in January. El-Sayed, 42, defeated Republican Mike Rogers on November 3, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the […]  The post  New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Howard Cooper — Abdul Al-Sayed (wikipedia commons) Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, says he plans to take his oath of office on a Quran when the new Congress convenes in January. El-Sayed, 42, defeated Republican Mike Rogers on November 3, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the Senate and the first epidemiologist to serve in the chamber, according to WION News. In an interview with NPR’s Leila Fadel, he said, “I will likely swear on a Quran. Which Quran, we’re not sure.” He pointed to a copy once owned by Thomas Jefferson, which Keith Ellison used when he was sworn in to Congress, and to an old Quran at the University of Michigan that he described as the first in the state. The US Constitution does not require a Bible or any religious text. In practice, senators usually take the formal oath together on the Senate floor, and a Bible comes into play in individual ceremonial swearings-in. El-Sayed hasn’t said whether he’ll use the Quran in the formal proceedings, the ceremony, or both, and that his choice would not alter the wording of the oath. He has also stressed that his oath will be to the U.S. Constitution,  according to IBTimes. He will be sworn in by Vice President JD Vance, a fact El-Sayed has noted with humor. The Blaze reported he called it a “delicious irony” that Vance is constitutionally required to do so. Not everyone is comfortable with the news. The Daily Signal reported that former White House press secretary Sean Spicer said this week that given El-Sayed’s connections and statements, he should undergo a formal background check before receiving classified information. Presumably, Spicer was referring to Al-Sayed’s family connections to the Muslim Brotherhood. For many Christians, the moment raises questions about the role of faith in public life, the long American tradition of religious liberty, and the Judeo-Christian roots of the United States. El-Sayed and his colleagues are scheduled to be sworn in at noon on January 3, 2027. The post New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran first appeared on God Reports .

summary: By Charles Gardner — A brave Yemeni journalist has stunned the United Nations with an account of how his view of Israel has dramatically changed following a visit there. Luai Ahmed was invited to […]  The post  Yemeni journalist visits Israel, dramatically changes views  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Charles Gardner — Luai Ahmed speaking at UN (screenshot YouTube) A brave Yemeni journalist has stunned the United Nations with an account of how his view of Israel has dramatically changed following a visit there. And he was led to the conclusion that everything he has been taught to believe about the Jews is a lie. Luai Ahmed was invited to address the assembly by UN Watch, a non-governmental organisation monitoring the international body’s performance, as the UN Human Rights Council gathered to debate racism. He said: “I grew up in Yemen, where the word that we used for black people is ‘abeed’, which quite literally means ‘slaves’. Racism towards black people in my country is horrifying, but it’s not even the most toxic hatred that I was taught. “The first time I ever heard the word ‘Jew’ was in my local mosque when I was nine years old. At the end of Friday prayers, the Imam said: ‘May Allah kill the Jews and the Zionists’. And I responded alongside thousands of Muslims praying beside me: ‘Ameen’.” Luai then continued: “I was taught that Zionism meant killing Arabs, stealing our land, and destroying Islam. Then October 7th came. Hamas terrorists ‘freed Palestine’ by slaughtering 1,200 Israelis and kidnapping more than 200 people, including a one-year-old child. “Almost everyone in my Arab-Muslim circle celebrated. I didn’t. Instead, as a journalist, I decided to visit the so-called Zionist entity, and I was completely shocked to the core by the lack of apartheid and racism that I experienced. “One day, I got an eye infection. At the hospital, the nurses in reception were Jewish. The doctor treating me was Arab. Is there racism in Israel? Of course. There’s racism everywhere. “But Arabs in Israel aren’t called ‘slaves’. They are doctors, engineers, and party leaders. My experience helped me realise that Zionism really just means the Jewish people’s right to a tiny country. Everything I was taught was a lie.” Quite apart from tipping over the tables of woke left-wing ideology spreading its poisonous antisemitic tentacles across the globe, Luai’s testimony also knocks holes into the escalating pressure on the UK to make reparations for the slave trade, which saw plenty of collaborators in the host countries of those who suffered. And of course, the truth that dare not speak its name – that it was Christians like William Wilberforce who put an end to it! Luai is a great inspiration to fellow journalists like me who long for more of our colleagues to stand up and be counted. Thanks also to David Soakell of Christian Friends of Israel’s Watching Over Zion newsletter, November 5, 2026. title: Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin
summary: By Mark Ellis — Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, […]  The post  Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Mark Ellis — Amber Sparks (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, especially with the Rigs-to-Reefs program, when oil drilling platforms are decommissioned. “We work with the oil companies to repurpose certain parts of the platform, retrofit it so that it can remain in place and continue to function as an artificial reef,” she told God Reports. Amber’s work has taken her around the world, with many dive experiences and encounters in the ocean with marine life. But there is one story she will never forget. It happened in the Gulf of Mexico shortly after Amber graduated from Scripps Institute and was invited on a research industry cruise with oil company representatives, scientists, and regulators on a liveaboard vessel. At the Flower Garden National Banks, a marine protected area 200 miles offshore, Amber was excited about her first dive, but slightly nervous. “You don’t know what you’re going to see or what this experience is going to be like,” she recalls. Dropping in (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook) Each diver had to jump off the vessel to get in the water. “We’re all geared up with our snorkel, our buoyancy control device, our wetsuit, and fins are the last thing you put on. So, I put on my fins and I jumped off the side of the boat.” “The second that I hit the water, one of my fins fell off, and I looked down and watched as it slowly descended to the bottom.” Amber glanced over at her dive buddy, and said, “I’m gonna go down. I’m going down.” Normally she would wait for her dive partner and they would go down together, but in this case, she thought, “I can’t (wait). I gotta go get my fin.” So Amber slowly began to descend to the bottom, about 60 feet below the ocean surface. “I felt completely lost. I was in a completely new area. I never dove before, and now I only had one fin.” She realized there were major currents that could have moved her fin in any direction. “I realized I can’t really swim with just one fin. So now not only am I at depth, but I’m handicapped with just one fin, and I started to feel pretty nervous.” It would probably take her 10 minutes to get back the surface, with safety stops. At the moment before panic set in, she looked upward and saw an amazing sight. It was a giant manta ray, with wings extending at least 10 feet. “Its wingspan was double mine. Its arms were out, and it was coming up over the side of a reef. “I’ve never seen a manta ray like this before. It totally took my breath away, it was so magnificent.” Another manta ray (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) She noted that manta rays are known in the ocean community to be “majestic, God-connected creatures with an understanding maybe beyond what humans can fully comprehend. They see the world and feel it in another way,” she notes. Mantas have the largest known brain of any fish. Their brains are large in absolute terms and relative to body size, which is also true of elephants, dolphins, and people. Their brains have enlarged areas associated with intelligence, vision, and motor coordination, and some of their brain cells are more like those in birds and mammals than in other fish.(1) As the manta ray drew close to Amber, she had an unusual communication experience. “I felt this sense where it said, ‘I want you to follow me. I’m going to help you find your fin.’ Amber Sparks Amber’s diving partner had just descended next to her, and they both began to swim after the manta. “I was barely making it, following this manta ray across the reef. At this point, I was so excited to see a manta ray. I kind of forgot about being handicapped, and I was just trying to go as fast as I can to keep up with it. Then Amber got the sur

content: The word epiphany is defined by the Oxford Learner’s Dictionary as “a sudden and surprising moment of understanding.” Often, such epiphany moments arrive unexpectedly, interrupting the ordinary rhythms of life with extraordinary insight. Sometimes they come through a conversation, a passage of Scripture, or an encounter with nature. Other times, they emerge through art. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Eliott Davis Sitting beneath artist James Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany on the campus of Rice University in Houston, Texas, on a Sunday morning as the sun rose, the word epiphany took on new meaning. As the morning light slowly illuminated the sky, subtle shifts in color transformed the space above me. The experience was both architectural and atmospheric, a convergence of art, nature, and contemplation. Turrell, born in 1943, is an American artist internationally recognized for his exploration of light, space, and human perception. Raised in the Quaker tradition, Turrell’s artistic vision reflects an appreciation for silence, stillness, and inward reflection. Commissioned by Rice University through the generosity of alumna Suzanne Deal Booth, Twilight Epiphany opened in 2012 as part of the university’s public art program. The pyramidal Skyspace, designed to accommodate approximately 120 visitors, features an aperture in its roof through which viewers observe the changing sky. At sunrise and sunset, carefully programmed LED lights interact with the natural atmosphere, creating an extraordinary experience of shifting color and perception. More than a work of architecture, the installation invites visitors to slow down, look upward, and reconsider the relationship between light and the world around them. James Turrell (Chat GPT) For me, the experience was something of a spiritual exercise. Light, after all, is among the Bible’s most enduring metaphors for divine revelation, truth, and beauty. As the colors shifted above me, I was reminded that beauty does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it simply asks us to be still and pay attention. Rothko Chapel. Photo: https://www.mark-rothko.org/rothko-chapel.jsp#google_vignette. From Rice University, I headed to another meditative landmark: the Rothko Chapel . Here, I sat among the monumental, dark-hued paintings of Mark Rothko, contemplating both the tragedy of the artist’s life and the triumph of the chapel that bears his name. Commissioned by Houston philanthropists John and Dominique de Menil in 1964 and dedicated in 1971, the Rothko Chapel is an interfaith sanctuary devoted to contemplation, spiritual reflection, and human rights. Its octagonal interior contains fourteen large-scale paintings by Rothko, whose subtle variations of black, maroon, and purple create an atmosphere of profound stillness. Rothko, born Marcus Rothkowitz in 1903, was a leading figure in American Abstract Expressionism, celebrated for his ability to evoke deep emotional responses through color and form. Yet his personal life was marked by physical illness, depression, and emotional turmoil. In February 1970, before the chapel’s dedication, Rothko died by suicide at the age of sixty-six. He never witnessed the completed sanctuary that would become one of his most enduring artistic legacies. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Brian C. Nixon There is something deeply moving about this juxtaposition. An artist whose life ended in despair left behind a place where countless visitors have sought peace, meaning, and solace. The darkness of Rothko’s paintings does not necessarily communicate hopelessness. Rather, their quiet intensity invites viewers to confront the depths of human experience—sorrow, longing, mystery, and perhaps even transcendence. Where Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany draws the eyes upward toward the heavens, Rothko’s chapel seems to draw the gaze inward, toward the mysteries of the human soul. title: Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success
summary: While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence […]  The post  Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: John Warwick Montgomery While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence with C. S. Lewis and his barrister gowns to the thousands of books that comprise his remarkable personal collection, Lanier has provided the Christian world with a marvelous tribute to one of the great Christian intellectuals of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Born in 1931, John Warwick Montgomery (d. 2024) was a distinguished Christian apologist, theologian, attorney, and scholar whose extraordinary career spanned several disciplines. Holding numerous academic degrees, including doctorates in theology, philosophy, and law, Montgomery became internationally recognized for his defense of Christianity through historical evidence, legal reasoning, and philosophical argumentation. His influential books, including History and Christianity , Faith Founded on Fact , and The Shape of the Past , helped establish a rigorous approach to Christian apologetics. Whether lecturing in universities, debating skeptics, or practicing law, Montgomery maintained that Christianity was not merely a matter of subjective belief but a faith grounded in historical reality and rational inquiry. Yet to stop at the library would be to understate Lanier’s remarkable work. The sixth annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series was a tour de force of distinguished thinkers, passionate Christians, and intellectually engaging presentations. More than a commemoration of Montgomery’s life, the gathering represented a continuation of his intellectual legacy: the conviction that Christianity can withstand serious scrutiny and offer compelling answers to life’s most profound questions. Mark Lanier, Nancy Pearcey, Paul Gould, Adam Francisco, and Michael Horton From the opening panel discussion hosted by attorney and philanthropist Mark Lanier to Dr. Paul Gould’s thoughtful presentation on worldviews, followed by attorney Craig Parton’s lecture on jurisprudential apologetics, one theme emerged with unmistakable clarity: Christianity is a reasonable faith. The presentations reflected Montgomery’s own interdisciplinary approach to apologetics: the Christian faith and intellectual inquiry need not be adversaries. Indeed, the Christian tradition has long insisted that faith and reason are complementary avenues in the pursuit of truth. The following day continued this rich intellectual exploration. Professor Nancy Pearcey addressed questions surrounding truth, dismantling various modern ideologies, while Dr. Adam Francisco offered an informative overview of Islamic history and belief, helping participants better understand one of world’s biggest religions. The keynote address by Dr. Michael Horton examined the challenge of reaching those who identify as “spiritual but not religious,” a growing segment of contemporary society. Horton’s presentation underscored the importance of communicating historic Christian truth in a culture increasingly suspicious of religious institutions yet often deeply interested in spiritual meaning. Dr. Michael Horton On Sunday morning, Lanier founder, Mark Lanier, hosted many participants during his Biblical literacy class, where he continued the dialogue with Michael Horton. Taken together, the lectures, discussions, and interviews demonstrated the breadth of Christian scholarship and the continuing relevance of thoughtful apologetics in an age of skepticism, religious pluralism, and cultural uncertainty. content: What do Jesus and Isaiah have in common? Quite a bit, according to renowned British New Testament scholar N. T. Wright. Gathering at the marvelous Lanier Theological Library in Houston, Texas—the brainchild of noted attorney, author, and biblical scholar Mark Lanier—Wright offered a packed house in the Great Room a fascinating glimpse into the relationship between the Old Testament prophet Isaiah and the life, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Dr. Joseph Holden of Veritas International University listening to Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. For Wright, Isaiah is far more than an ancient prophetic voice whose words occasionally appear in the New Testament. Rather, the prophet provides a theological framework for understanding Jesus and the unfolding purposes of God. In his book Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright invites readers to rediscover the extraordinary depth of Isaiah’s prophetic vision, demonstrating how its themes of judgment, restoration, redemption, and new creation find their ultimate expression in Christ. Central to Wright’s interpretation is the conviction that Isaiah’s message cannot be separated from the larger story of Israel. The prophet speaks of exile and homecoming, divine judgment and covenant faithfulness, suffering and salvation. These themes, Wright argues, become essential to understanding how Jesus understood his own mission and how the earliest Christians interpreted his life. Particularly significant is Isaiah’s portrayal of the suffering servant, whose affliction becomes the means through which God’s redemptive purposes are accomplished. Wright connects this prophetic imagery to Jesus’ sacrificial death, while emphasizing that the cross cannot be isolated from the broader biblical promise of God’s restoration of creation. Equally important is Isaiah’s vision of a renewed world, a creation in which justice, righteousness, and peace flourish under God’s reign. For Wright, the resurrection of Jesus announces the beginning of that promised new creation. The Christian hope, therefore, is not simply an escape from the present world, but the ultimate renewal of God’s good creation. Personal Stories: Mounting Up with Wings Like Eagles Amid the theological insights and biblical exposition, Wright shared several personal stories, offering the audience a glimpse into how the words of Isaiah have shaped not only his scholarship but also his spiritual imagination. One story centered on the beloved passage from Isaiah 40:31, in which the prophet declares that those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles. Wright recalled preaching on Isaiah many years earlier and drew an amusing comparison to the long-running British radio program Desert Island Discs , in which notable guests select the recordings they would take with them if stranded on a deserted island. “I’ve sometimes said I have a set of desert island texts,” Wright explained, suggesting that certain biblical passages remain especially meaningful throughout one’s life. Near the top of his list, he said, is the closing portion of Isaiah 40, with its magnificent image of soaring eagles. The passage, he suggested, is more than a favorite theological text. It is part of his personal testimony, a biblical promise that has accompanied him through the years. A second story brought the imagery of Isaiah into an unexpected encounter with the natural world. While completing the final proofreading of Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright and his wife, Maggie, were staying at their home in Scotland. Wright was alone in a room, carefully reviewing the text, when something outside caught his attention. “Out of the corner of my eye, I saw something,” he recalled. “At first, I thought it was somebody’s dog that had come into our front garden.” Noted Biblical archeologist, Dr. Steven Collins, listening to Mark Lanier interview Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. content: By Charles Gardner — When a Japanese sailor’s destroyer was sunk by the Americans in a World War II South Pacific battle, most of his companions drowned. Amazingly, even though he was sucked underneath the waves with others as the ship went down, torpedo officer Michiharu Shinya somehow survived this 1942 disaster. (Only 18 of the 200-strong crew did). But he would rather have died at that point as his people had been indoctrinated to believe that it was shameful to be captured. Nevertheless, he was badly wounded but nursed back to health by medics. In time, he was picked up and eventually taken to a Prisoner-of-War camp at Featherston, near Wellington, in New Zealand, where he was to spend the next three years, as Don Stephens records in his inspirational book War and Grace (Evangelical Press, an imprint of 10Publishing). Shinya and his fellow inmates were treated with much kindness (in sharp contrast to the torture often experienced by Allied prisoners at the hands of the Japanese). Being showered with gifts at Christmas, a feast he knew nothing about, seemed especially strange. However, he was determined not to be ‘taken in’ by the Christian teaching offered after some of the prisoners requested spiritual help and a Japanese Bible was made available. That is until he chanced upon an article entitled ‘Sorrow in Victory’ in which the author quoted a ‘Hebrew prophet’ as saying: “Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They shall soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not be faint.” It made a deep impression on him, and he was determined to find out where it came from. Assuming it was from the Old Testament, he began reading the Bible, starting at Genesis chapter 1. Eventually, to his joy, he discovered that the profound words were from the Book of the prophet Isaiah (chapter 40, verse 31). After flagging somewhat in his search, he found himself hospitalised with malaria when a friend brought him a booklet called The Reason Why explaining the way to salvation. It so happened that the camp’s chaplain, Pastor Hessell Troughton, had been a missionary to Japan and spoke the language. Shinya joined others in his Bible studies and came to know and love Jesus as his Saviour. So much did this “complete freedom” now rule his life that prison had morphed into what he described as “a unique paradise on earth”. He never looked back after that and became convinced that his post-war calling would be in service of his Lord. When he finally returned home, his family were shocked to see him alive for he had been reported as killed in action. He had also given a false name to his captors because of the supposed shame of falling into enemy hands. Shinya subsequently became a pastor and prolific writer and translator following years of theological study both in Tokyo and the US. The Old Testament, he came to believe, demonstrated that sin is “the ultimate problem of mankind” and clearly pointed to Christ as the answer. On seeking to understand why so few Japanese became Christians, he felt it was partly due to their pride borne of believing they were a superior race. As for those three Christmases he spent in New Zealand, author Don Stephens writes: “Of all the gifts he received, the one he valued most was ‘the boundless and deep grace and peace of God in the Lord Jesus Christ’.” The post WWII Japanese POW found ‘freedom’ in camp first appeared on God Reports .

title: In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words
summary: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star, the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of […]  The post  In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star , the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of one of America’s most celebrated novelists. Having written about McMurtry’s faith—or lack thereof—in a previous article , following an earlier visit to Archer City, I’m returning with a somewhat different interest. This time, my attention turns to Grover Lewis, the gifted journalist, critic, and poet whose life intersected with McMurtry’s during their college years. Lewis’ story, however, begins not with literary achievement but with almost unimaginable tragedy. As a child, he experienced the devastating loss of both parents when his father murdered his mother and was subsequently shot with the same gun, either by his dying wife or another person present. Lewis was only eight years old. It is difficult to imagine a more horrific beginning. Yet rather than allowing that tragedy to become the entirety of his story, Lewis eventually found a voice through literature. Perhaps the cards life dealt him gave him plenty to write about. Or perhaps writing became his way of making sense of a world that had revealed its cruelty far too early. In his autobiographical poem “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis writes: “You asked me once, Ann/Over coffee gone cold with talk/In your mother’s rain-drowsy/House, who they were, how it/Was with them in their breathless/Time in the wilds of years.” For Lewis, those early years were indeed wild. But they were also the soil from which his literary imagination would eventually grow. A Life in Words Born in Texas in 1934, Grover Lewis emerged as a distinctive voice in American journalism, particularly through his cultural criticism and reporting on the rapidly changing landscape of the 1960s and 1970s. He became known for his sharp observations, literary flair, and ability to capture the personalities and contradictions of American culture, even if he occasionally stretched the truth in the telling. His work appeared in prominent publications, including Rolling Stone , where his reporting helped establish his reputation as an insightful, sometimes cutting observer of popular culture. Lewis was more than a journalist, however. He was a poet and literary craftsman, someone who understood that words could do more than convey information. They could illuminate the human condition, expose its contradictions, and perhaps even provide a measure of healing. Grover Lewis (ChatPGT) Continuing “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis ponders: “At last, breathless and dry-mouthed/With private desire in the blue,/Swollen dark, we all lie down together—/My mother, my father, their perishing/Dreams, and I this unborn prisoner son…” There is something haunting about these lines. The dead remain present. The past refuses to disappear. And the poet, even as an adult, seems to wrestle with the circumstances that shaped his entrance into the world. Yet the very act of writing suggests something else: a refusal to remain silent. Two Texans, Two Literary Paths Lewis and Larry McMurtry crossed paths as students at North Texas State College, now the University of North Texas, during the 1950s. Both were young Texans drawn to literature and the possibilities of the written word. Their friendship developed within a shared intellectual environment, one that encouraged reading, conversation, and the pursuit of literary ambitions. Although their careers eventually followed different paths—McMurtry toward novels, screenplays, and literary fame, Lewis toward journalism, poetry, and cultural criticism—they shared an interest in the complexities of American life. content: Pastor Peter Colon portraying Major Rossvally in the movie of his story By Charles Gardner — A Jewish army surgeon was amazed by the courage of a young soldier badly wounded in the Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War (1861-65). Dr Max Rossvally was forced to amputate both a leg and arm in a bid to save the boy’s life. But it changed his own life. For the 17-year-old Drummer Boy – too young for frontline duty – refused chloroform or brandy to dull the pain. Charlie Coulson chose instead to trust in Jesus, his Lord and Saviour. The doctor – an army major and Orthodox Jew – was understandably stunned by the boy’s bravery, as well as his boldness in declaring his faith in Christ and imploring the officer (whom he knew to be Jewish) to put his own trust in Jesus, since he was also the Jewish Messiah. Max, however, was shaken rigid, and in a great dilemma, as he had always been taught to hate Jesus. For his people had largely rejected him as an ‘impostor’ and false Messiah. Charlie died just days later, apparently more concerned for the doctor’s eternal destiny than for his own painful exit from this life. Ten years later, Max found himself in a barber’s chair in New York once more being urged to trust in Jesus. Having explained the gospel, the barber promised to pray for him and said that, whenever he came in contact with a Jew, he felt it his duty to introduce him to the one who came for “the lost sheep of Israel” (Matthew 10:6). The surgeon subsequently boarded a train for a business meeting in Washington, where a newspaper advertisement drew him to a ‘revival’ service where the preacher echoed the messages he had heard from the barber and the boy soldier, leaving him in tears. He agonised at home in prayer for some time afterwards, struggling most of all with the thought that, if he accepted Christ, he would be going against all the advice and teaching he had known, not to mention the Jewish community as a whole. But he finally became convinced that Jesus was indeed the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecies (in particular, Genesis 49:10, Micah 5:2 and Isaiah 7:14). So he prayed: “O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. You know I am sincere in this thing. If Jesus Christ is the Son of God, reveal him to me this night, and I will accept him as my Messiah.” A long battle ensued, but his doubts were eventually replaced by joy and happiness as he praised God that he had found the true Shiloh, Ruler of Israel and Emmanuel. He was to pay a high price, however, as do all who follow Christ. His wife walked out on him; his parents disowned him. But he never gave up hope as he constantly prayed and reached out to his family. After 54 days, his wife joined him as a disciple of Jesus and, in time, his daughter also became a believer. But his son disowned him for many years until he was eventually reconciled both with his earthly and heavenly Father. In an extraordinary sequel some 18 months after he came to Christ, Max met up with Mrs Coulson, the mother of his dying young patient all those years earlier on the battlefield. With great joy, he was able to share how her son had set him on the path to a glorious future in Christ, which was to touch lives across the world, including my home county of Yorkshire in England. In fact, he came to live in Leeds to reach out to the Jewish community there and is buried at Lawnswood Cemetery in the city. An Irish friend of mine, Colin Nevin, has visited the grave, which includes an excerpt from one of the doctor’s hymns, I am Coming Soon, and was able to give a copy of Max’s story to a caretaker, so continuing the evangelist’s legacy more than a century after his death in 1892, aged 64. A 54-minute movie – Rossvally: From the Synagogue to the Saviour – has been produced on DVD and can apparently be ordered online. content: By Charles Gardner — We used to be regular viewers of the The Great British Bake-Off TV series, now being screened on Channel 4, celebrating the efforts of amateur contestants in the kitchen. My wife is qualified in home economics and once, in her far-off student days, helped Mary Berry out over the weekend. I too like to lend a hand with my cooking skills. So when, the other day, we were intrigued to see how new presenter Nigella Lawson was doing on the show, we switched it on – and were truly appalled at the foul language spewing out of the mouths of at least two contestants. Taking the name of the Lord Jesus Christ in vain, they loudly expressed their frustration (rather than praise) at things going wrong with their concoctions in front of more than seven million viewers. We switched it off, vowing to complain in the strongest possible terms, which I have since done. And though it’s hard to be surprised at the language regularly heard on television programmes these days, I was shocked to the core by Channel 4’s response, basically saying that this particularly offensive blasphemy doesn’t come under the category of “strong language”. Really? It’s surely the worst of them all. “We are sorry to hear you were offended by some of the language used within the programme,” they wrote. “Whilst we do appreciate that you find the use of such phrases or words unacceptable, we are not obliged under the Ofcom code to obscure them, nor do they fall under the category for strong language. We therefore have no obligation to bleep them either pre- or post-watershed.” I had suggested that they could at least have edited them out, adding that they were being very hypocritical as they wouldn’t have allowed swearing in the name of Mohammed, a point which they ignored. Have we sunk so low in our nation that there is nothing left that is sacred, except woke left-wing ideology and appeasement of those who hate the God of Israel and his Son Jesus, our Lord? But we have forsaken the God who brought peace and prosperity to Britain, and who saved us from Nazi invasion, for the idols of food and celebrity. Shame on us! Is it not time the Christian world woke up and stood against this flood of filth in our midst, which will sweep us away into the oblivion of a third-rate country if we do not act soon. Where has the ‘land of hope and glory’ gone? The ‘mother of the free’ we sing about at the Proms, calling on the God ‘who made thee mighty’ to ‘make thee mightier yet’? The Apostle Paul was surely prophesying the decline and fall of the Roman Empire in his letter to the early Christians in Rome (a mixture of Jews and Gentiles), when he wrote: “The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the truth by their wickedness, since what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities – his eternal power and divine nature – have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made, so that men are without excuse.” (Romans 1:18-20) The post Offended by foul language on food show first appeared on God Reports .

title: Two truck tires and a white dove taught me to trust God

content: By Mike Shreve — Tent meeting in the 80s Evangelism has been my focus for 55 years, ministering throughout the United States and in 14 other nations. God mercifully saved me during the Jesus Revolution (1970), out of a hippie lifestyle and a passionate, though misguided pursuit of truth through far eastern religious practices (yoga and meditation). Shortly after encountering Jesus and being delivered, along with another brother in the Lord, I began hitchhiking around the country, preaching the Gospel on street corners and college campuses. That developed through the years into ministry in churches, auditoriums, conferences, and tent crusades. Supernatural provision and divine intervention has always carried me, through every phase of this five-and-a-half-decade-long adventure. However, the following story is a classic. For about 25 years I carried big Gospel tents around the country. At the time of this “miracle,” I was transporting a 60’ x 90’ tent from one city to the next in an old, dilapidated bus that kept introducing new challenges to our amateur mechanic skills (putting it mildly). One day, on our way to Tampa, Florida—unfortunately—we hit a large pothole in the road that put a serious dent in the rear left rim on which a large truck tire was mounted. From that point, the inner tube would not retain air, making it necessary to stop every thirty miles or so to fill it up again . . . and again . . . and again . . . making the trip painfully slow. Adding to the problem, the other rear tire was bald, and we had no spare (couldn’t afford one). So, a flat would have brought us to a complete standstill. Sometimes, I think back on those days (when our zeal for the Kingdom outran any wisdom we might have possessed), and I marvel at the many times God took care of us anyway (like the loving heavenly Father that He is). Thousands of pounds of equipment were packed into that groaning, creaking, rusty, decrepit bus — heavy canvas tent sections, metal poles, stakes, platform, and 300 chairs—and only a few days allowed in between cities for transit and setup. No, we really could not afford any setbacks. And yes, a lot of “faith prayers” were uttered during every trip (or were they “presumptive proclamations”—not sure—maybe a mix of the two). An old split rim tire mounted on an old bus Once we got to Tampa, attempting to be frugal, I visited the junkyards hoping to find a used replacement rim. As if they had conspired to dissuade me, every junkyard owner/manager shot down my hopes with a similar assessment, “Fella, you won’t find one of them old split-rims anywhere. They’re dangerous. When you try to mount a tire on one, they can snap open and injure somebody real bad, cutting off a hand, even killing a person. We melted ‘em all down as scrap metal.” (Go ahead, look them up online—they were even called “widow-makers.”) It was the same story everywhere I went. Nobody could help. Then three weeks passed and we had to pack the bus and head to our next location—Bessemer City, North Carolina. It was a college-level, biblically-sound course on developing long-suffering and patience: stopping every thirty miles or so to air up that unpredictable tire, pleading with God to somehow supernaturally assist us in our journey by making sure none of the tires blew. Somehow, we made it—around 600 miles—stopping about 25 times. Then an incredible miracle happened! God did it and I still feel awestruck, just writing about it. As we turned into the fairgrounds area, right in the middle of the entrance were two brand new, neatly-stacked truck tires (unclaimed), exactly the size we used on the bus—mounted (you guessed it!) on the very same split rims our bus required. Talk about worshiping God—we launched into a praise session right then and there! What were the odds? We all knew it had to be God. title: Spiritual fighter pilots needed for new Battle for Britain!
summary: By Charles Gardner — The Battle of Britain, which saw Spitfires and Hurricanes save us from Nazi invasion and ensure our freedom, apparently ended after three months on October 31, 1940.
